summary: Defines the forwarding element model for ForCES, which describes a forwarding element's functions, capabilities, state and configuration, and how those functions connect. Control elements use it to control the forwarding elements. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5812 defines a model for describing what a ForCES forwarding element can do and how its functions are connected. A control element uses the model to discover capabilities and manage configuration.

questions: how does forces describe an fe
what is a logical functional block
what is the forces forwarding element model
subtitle: A model that lets a ForCES controller discover and configure a forwarding element.

tldr.problem: ForCES forwarding elements can have different capabilities, so a control element needs a shared model for discovering their functions, state, and configuration.
tldr.mechanism: The model represents an FE as Logical Functional Blocks connected in a directed graph. XML class definitions describe each block's ports, components, capabilities, events, and metadata.
tldr.outcome: The model provides a vocabulary for ForCES protocol exchanges, but defines only the FE Object block. The unit metadata says RFC 7408 updates this RFC.

today: RFC 5812 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2010. The unit metadata says it was updated by RFC 7408.

sections.title: Why ForCES Needs a Forwarding Element Model
sections.content:
ForCES separates control elements (CEs), which decide how traffic should be handled, from forwarding elements (FEs), which process packets. FEs may differ in function, so a CE needs to discover an FE's capabilities and current state before controlling it.

RFC 5812 defines the FE model used for this description. It is mainly an information model, with explicit schema for LFB classes and FEs. The ForCES protocol uses it as the basis for information exchanged between CEs and FEs.
sections.plainLanguage: A control element needs to know what each forwarding element supports before it can configure it. This RFC defines a shared way to describe that information.

sections.title: Capabilities, State and Logical Functional Blocks
sections.content:
The model distinguishes capabilities, state, and configuration. Capabilities describe what an FE can support and its limits; state describes what it is doing now; configuration describes what the CE requests.

A Logical Functional Block (LFB) performs a distinct function on packets, such as classification, metering, shaping, or marking. An LFB can also hold control information, as the FE Object does. A class definition describes the LFB components and the information visible to the CE.
sections.plainLanguage: Capabilities describe what a forwarding element can do, while state describes what it is doing now. LFBs represent the separate functions that process packets or hold control information.

sections.title: Ports, Packets and Metadata
sections.content:
An LFB input and output carries a packet, metadata, or both. Metadata is per-packet information passed between LFBs; the model represents it as a named value. A class definition says which packet types its ports accept or produce and which metadata they read, create, change, or consume.

An output connects to one input, while several outputs may connect to one input. LFB classes can use fixed separate outputs or an output group when the number of paths varies. Input groups can identify which input instance delivered a packet.
sections.plainLanguage: LFB ports pass packets with associated metadata from one function to another. The model describes which inputs and outputs can connect and what information each one carries.

sections.title: Events, Versions and Inheritance
sections.content:
An LFB can define events, such as a link failure, that it reports to the CE when the CE subscribes. The ForCES protocol defines the event message format. Each LFB class definition also has a version.

A new LFB class may inherit from a base class. It can add components but cannot remove inherited ones, and a class cannot use multiple inheritance. The model permits vendors to extend standardized LFBs while giving a CE a way to query the base class of an LFB it does not recognize.
sections.plainLanguage: An LFB can report defined events to a control element that subscribes to them. A new class can extend a base class, but it must preserve the base class's components.

sections.title: Addressing Model Components
sections.content:
The model uses 32-bit identifiers for an FE, an LFB class, an LFB instance, and a component. An instance identifier is unique within its class on that FE; a class identifier is global within the network element.

Components can be nested or arranged in tables. A dot-separated path identifies nested components and table entries, and a table may also allow the CE to select an entry by its contents using keys.
sections.plainLanguage: A CE addresses a component by identifying its FE, LFB class, LFB instance, and component. Paths and table keys let it identify nested values precisely.

sections.title: LFB Topology and Packet Paths
sections.content:
LFB topology is a directed graph of the logical packet paths inside an FE. Nodes represent LFB instances; links show the direction in which packets flow. It describes logical processing, not the physical arrangement of hardware.

The model can express different packet treatment with separate paths or with metadata that downstream blocks use to select behavior. A mix is often useful: explicit paths suit distinct functions that change infrequently, while attributes suit choices that change often. An FE may restrict whether its topology can be changed.
sections.plainLanguage: The topology graph shows which LFB functions process a packet and in what order. Designers can represent different treatment as separate paths, metadata-driven choices, or a combination.

sections.title: The FE Object and CE Interaction
sections.content:
Every FE has one FEObject instance, with class ID 1 and instance ID 1. A CE can read this known object to learn about the FE, its supported LFB classes, topology limits, current state, and configured neighbors. Class ID 2 is reserved for the FEProtocol object.

The ForCES protocol uses the model to query FE and LFB topology, discover capabilities and state, manipulate components, and reconfigure topology. This RFC defines the FE Object class; other LFB class definitions are provided separately.
sections.plainLanguage: The FE Object is the known place where a CE reads information about an FE and its LFBs. The ForCES protocol uses that information for queries and configuration changes.
